Your learning goals

By the end of this lesson,
you can…

Use these goals to guide your exploration and check what you have learned.

  • Explain foresight: describe how exploring several possible futures can help us make decisions today.
  • Separate evidence from speculation: identify real technology signals, research ideas and imagined future scenarios.
  • Follow the data: explain how a sensor can connect a physical object to a digital system, and compare local processing with cloud processing.
  • Explore consequences: compare different choices and explain who could benefit, who could be left out and what might happen next.
  • Test and revise a plan: change a design choice, explore an unexpected event and explain why the result changes.
  • Plan for a preferred future: work backwards to suggest an action we can take today and a signal to monitor.
  • Justify your thinking in English: use evidence and phrases such as “This could…”, “This depends on…” and “An alternative future might…” to explain your choices.
01 / Think in futures

The future is plural.

Foresight means exploring several possible futures so we can make better decisions now. It is not a promise about what will happen.

Start with what you see • 5 minutes

Notice. Wonder. Discuss.

You do not need to know the word foresight yet. Look at the image, think quietly for 30 seconds, then share your ideas with a partner.

  1. Notice: What are the first three things you notice? What words or feelings come to mind?
  2. Wonder: What might the telescope, the mist and the branching paths represent?
  3. Imagine: Why might there be several paths instead of one? Could the brightest path still have problems?
  4. Connect: Imagine the paths show how we might use devices in ten years. What could two different paths look like?
  5. Act: What could people do today to influence which paths become possible? What might remain beyond their control?

You can discuss your answer instead of writing. Written thoughts are included in your notebook download.

After your discussion: how does this connect to foresight?

In everyday language: foresight means asking, “What different things could happen, and how can we prepare or help shape them?” We look for clues in the present, question our assumptions and explore more than one future.

  • The telescope: looking beyond what is immediately in front of us and searching for signs of change. It cannot show us exactly what will happen.
  • The mist: uncertainty. Some things are unclear, and surprises can change our plans.
  • The branching paths: different possible futures. Our choices, other people’s choices and wider events can influence which paths develop.

A familiar example: one future might combine smartphones with wearable devices. Another might favour simpler devices and fewer connected services. We can explore what would make each future plausible, who would benefit and what choices we could make now.

The image is a metaphor, not a map of tomorrow. The paths are not fixed, and a brighter path is not automatically better for everyone. Foresight helps us prepare for uncertainty; it does not remove it.

Try explaining it to a partner: “Foresight helps us explore… so that we can…”

01 / SIGNAL

What can we notice?

A real observation that may suggest change: for example, sensors becoming small enough to fit inside a ring.

02 / DRIVER

What pushes change?

A force such as cheaper electronics, pressure to reduce waste, new rules or a desire for convenience.

03 / UNCERTAINTY

What could go either way?

Will people trust always-available devices? Will they be affordable? Different answers create different futures.

04 / ACTION

What can we do now?

Test an idea, include people who might be left out and choose actions that help across several futures.

Possible ≠ probable ≠ preferable. Possible means it could happen. Plausible means there is a credible explanation for how. Probable means judged more likely, given evidence and assumptions. Preferable means someone wants it to happen. People can disagree about all four.

03 / Reality check

Signal or speculation?

Before imagining tomorrow, check what we actually know today.

Put the claim in its place.

Choose the strongest description of each statement. Read the explanation, then try the next one.

What do the categories mean?

Documented today: evidence supports its existence, but not necessarily widespread use.
Research: a project or prototype, with limits still to test.
Scenario: an invented future possibility.
Overclaim: a statement that goes beyond the evidence.

These questions check evidence reading. Your scenario choices are never scored.

04 / Follow the data

How does paper talk
to the cloud?

It needs a system. A sensor label is not automatically an internet-connected computer. Explore this simplified, hypothetical setup.

A measurement is not the same as an interpretation. A temperature reading alone cannot prove that food is safe. Some tags only identify an item; sensing requires additional materials or components.

05 / Experiment with change

What if the future
doesn’t follow your plan?

Make a prediction, change one choice and compare the consequences. These are simplified, rule-based thought experiments—not forecasts or measured real-world effects.

SIMULATION 1 / THE DEVICE LAUNCH

A pendant for the town library

A fictional library wants to lend a pendant that helps visitors remember book recommendations and find activities. You are on its design team. Build a pilot, then test it against an unexpected event.

Your task: predict a consequence, run the pilot, then change one design choice while keeping the event the same.

Which effect changes? What trade-off remains? Then try a different event to test your assumptions.

Your result will appear here.

Choose a design and an event, then run the pilot. Different configurations produce different consequences.

Look inside the model

Cloud-only functions stop during the model’s internet outage; local functions continue. Hybrid keeps only its basic functions. A breach is assumed to expose retained data, wherever it is stored. Cloud price rises affect cloud-only and hybrid designs. A pendant-only route leaves some visitors without a usable option. Alternatives require staffing; local and hybrid designs require maintenance. These are authored assumptions, not probabilities, cost estimates or a complete security model.

SIMULATION 2 / A PLAN THAT CAN ADAPT

Three actions. Four possible futures.

The library can prioritise three actions before expanding its pilot. Choose them, stress-test the same plan against four futures and then revise it. There is no plan that removes every trade-off.

For this classroom model, each action uses one of three planning slots. Real actions have unequal costs and take different amounts of time. This task is independent of your first pilot configuration.

0 of 3 planning slots used.

What does the stress test show?

The model checks whether your chosen actions address specific pressures in each fictional future. “Addressed” means a planned response exists—not that it has been proven effective. Gaps identify a discussion point, not a failed grade. Several combinations can be defensible. Test all four futures, include affected people and ask what evidence you would need before acting.

Simulation runs, tested plans and reflections are included in your downloadable notebook. They disappear if you refresh or close this page.

06 / Future studio

Change the assumptions.
Change the world.

Use two uncertainties to make four plausible story worlds. These are prompts for exploration, not a ranking.

Who gets access? Who has control?

Select a world. Access means affordability and availability. Control means meaningful choice over data and use.

Your preferred future

This is backcasting: start with a preferred future, then identify steps towards it. A useful plan also survives less desirable futures.

Field notes

A few useful words.

Internet of Things (IoT)

Physical objects connected to systems that collect or exchange data. A sensor can connect through a nearby reader or phone rather than directly to the internet.

Sensor

A component or material that responds to a physical condition, such as motion or temperature, producing a signal that can be read.

Cloud / edge computing

Cloud computing uses remote servers. Edge computing processes data nearer its source, for example on a phone or local gateway. Systems can combine both.

Inference

A conclusion drawn from data. A device may measure movement and infer sleep; the conclusion can be wrong.

Second-order consequence

What happens because of an initial effect. A faster service may reduce queues, then change staffing or exclude people who cannot use it.

Wildcard

A surprising event with a large impact. Use it to stress-test your plan: what if connectivity disappeared for a week?

Evidence desk — real signals behind the stories
  1. OECD — Strategic foresightExploring multiple plausible futures to inform decisions in the present.
  2. European Commission — Strategic foresightA futures lens and distinctions between kinds of futures.
  3. Oura — Technology in Oura Ring Gen3Manufacturer explanation of ring sensors. Supports the existence of sensing rings, not the fictional school use.
  4. Amazon — Bee wearable AI product descriptionA commercial example of a wearable designed to turn conversations into summaries. The pendant in our story is invented.
  5. MIT J-WAFS — Wireless RFID sensors for packagingA research project aiming to integrate pH-responsive materials with RFID labels. Not proof of universal commercial use.
  6. Ha and colleagues (2020) — Food and liquid sensing using RFIDsResearch demonstrating sensing with passive tags in specified settings; not a guarantee of safety for every food.
For teachers — lesson guidance

Learning goal: Students distinguish signals from speculation, explain a physical-to-digital data path, compare consequences and use backcasting to propose action. Suggested English level: B1–B2, with vocabulary support. Read aloud, work in pairs or discuss orally when helpful.

45–60 minutes: 5 minutes introducing foresight; 15–20 minutes exploring two missions and comparing routes; 10 minutes on claims and data; 10–15 minutes building a future; 5–10 minutes sharing notebooks. For a longer lesson, complete all four missions. Ask “What would have to be true?” and “Whose voice is missing?”
